blocks.p: Sumida was two changes and two hundred and thirty yen away. Rei watched the river go past under the train and counted the coins left on his IC card, because counting small things was what he had instead of sleep.

The man's name was Iwata. It was the same name as the handyman in Gin's building, which meant nothing. It was a common name. He opened the door of his Sumida flat already smiling. It was the particular wet-eyed smile Rei had learned to dread this week, the smile of a person who has been carried over water and does not yet know the boat is still beneath him. He was younger than the entry had made him sound, perhaps twenty-six. The flat behind him was the flat of a man who had just started living again. The dishes were done. A window was open. A photograph of someone gone had been turned at last to face the room instead of the wall.

"You're his brother," Iwata said, before Rei had said anything at all, and Rei's skin went cold. He had given this man no name. "He told me you'd come. He said you'd be tired, and that I should make you tea."

Rei sat, because to stand would be to flee. He took the tea, because refusing it would start the conversation with an accusation. Across the low table he watched a genuinely happy man explain what had happened. Three nights ago a soft-spoken stranger named Gin had found him at the river, where he had gone to do the thing the grief was steering him toward. And Gin had simply... Iwata's hands opened, helplessly grateful.
"He took the weight off," Iwata said. "He showed me how to set it down."

Iwata slept now. Iwata ate. Iwata had, he said with shining eyes, never felt so held in his life. Every true word of it landed in Rei like a nail. He had come here to show this man a leash. What he had found was a man who would have died on Saturday and was alive on Tuesday. And the thing that had saved him was the thing Rei had come to destroy.

Before he could stop himself, Rei took the silver coin from his pocket and set it on the table between the cups, as if he had been emptying his pockets and forgotten it. Iwata picked it up at once. He turned it over with real interest, read the old date, weighed it in his palm, and handed it back. Nothing in him flinched. Nothing rode him. Whatever the Healer had done here, it had not moved in. The reaction was the intelligence, Gin's page said, and the reaction was nothing at all.

Rei tried, gently, to find the seam another way. He asked whether Iwata had noticed anything he could not explain. Any debts he did not remember agreeing to. Any pull when he thought of the man who had helped him. He watched the question slide off Iwata like rain off oilcloth. He watched the gratitude close smoothly over the place where doubt should go. And he understood the engineering of it at last. The Healer did not bind people against their grief. It bound them through it. The leash was not laid over the wound. It was woven into the healing. To pull on the thread was to pull on the one thing keeping the person whole. No one could hate the hand that was also the stitches. Not Iwata. Not the widow. Not Rei.

It was not how Gin healed people. Rei knew that from the archive, from a page at the end of the chapter on suffering beings that Gin had plainly written for himself. After the hard work, Gin wrote, eat. Drink water. Do something entirely ordinary that needs full attention. Cooking something you actually care about, a conversation with someone you actually like. Find someone to sit with afterwards, and let the ordinary be ordinary for a while. The ordinariness is the protocol, Gin had written. Take it seriously. Gin's kind of healing sent a person back out into their own life, to their own table and their own people. The Healer's kind sent them back to the Healer.

Iwata was talking about work. He had gone back to the warehouse on Monday. His supervisor had said he looked like a new man. He laughed when he said it, a little embarrassed, and refilled Rei's cup though it was still half full. There was nothing in the flat that did not belong to an ordinary life. That was what made it unbearable.

He thought of the fourth rule in Gin's Grid chapter. Debt and reciprocity. When someone helps you, you help someone else. The Grid's debts were meant to move on, from one hand to the next, until nobody could say who had started it. Iwata's debt did not move. It ran in one direction only, back to the hand that had made it, and it would wait there for as long as the hand wanted.
Rei said his brother's name. He said Gin the way he had said it across a whole childhood. Soft. Claiming. The word he used to call him in from the dark.

blocks.cap: Iwata in Sumida, and the tenant still at work behind him

blocks.p: The flat changed temperature. Not Iwata. Iwata only tilted his head, still smiling, and asked if Rei was all right. It was the air that answered. The cheap fluorescent tube over the sink dimmed by a breath, as if something far away had leaned its weight against a wall. And at the back of Rei's own skull, behind the two registers he kept pressed flat, he felt the thread he had reached for reach back.

It was the first time all week the rope had had a near end as well as a far one. The Healer was on the line. Through Iwata's untouched contentment it had just felt Rei's hand close on its work. And it was... Rei would have sworn to this, in the heat, with his pulse loud in his ears... interested.

This was the thing the ledger could not teach him and the man at the river just had. A knot is not a knot. A knot is a place where the rope folds back on itself, and when one end is pulled, both lengths move. Rei had spent a week imagining himself outside the design, a reader standing over a map. In this small bright kitchen, with a saved man pouring him more tea, he finally felt the truth his sight had been muffling. The moment he touched a binding with love in his voice, he put love into the system. The Healer kept a ledger of love the way it kept a ledger of favours. Rei had just made an entry he could not unwrite. It knew his frequency now. It had been wanting it since the fourteenth.

He set the cup down before his hand could shake it. Across the table, Iwata's peace was undisturbed. Perfect. Sealed. That was the horror Rei would carry out of the door. The convert had felt nothing. The violence had run entirely between Rei and the thing in his brother, over the head of the man whose grief was the medium.

He had come to Sumida to free a knot. Instead he had proved that the rope ran both ways. That meant the Healer could be reached. It also meant the Healer could reach him. On the train home, with the coin back in his pocket and the river going past again underneath him, he no longer knew whether he was pulling it toward the light, or whether it was reeling him toward the post at Kita, one warm patient turn at a time.
